title: Tell the Sanhaja, Every One of Them
intro: Abu Ishaq al-Ilbiri addressed this poem to the Sanhaja, the Berber tribe of Badis ibn Habbus, the Zirid king of Granada, to turn them against the king's Jewish vizier, Joseph ibn Naghrela, who had succeeded his father Samuel as Badis's secretary and chief minister and who, as Inan and al-Daya tell it, had the poet exiled to Elvira; Ibn Sa'id says the poet had objected to the king's choice of a Jewish vizier. It opens by blaming the king for choosing a non-Muslim minister, sets the place of the Jews under earlier rulers against what the poet says he saw in Granada, Jewish officials collecting the taxes and the vizier living in luxury, and ends by calling for the vizier's killing and the seizure of his community's wealth, denying that killing them would be a breach of faith since, he argues, they had broken the pact that protected them. On Saturday 10 Safar 459 AH, the date the Tibyan gives (30 December 1066 CE), the soldiers and people of Granada rose against Joseph and killed him, then turned on the city's Jews, killing many and plundering their property; Ibn Bassam puts the dead at more than four thousand. The sources differ on the poem's part in this: Ibn Sa'id and al-Maqqari have the Sanhaja rising once it became known, Ibn Idhari, as Ibn al-Khatib quotes him, lists its spread among the events before the rising, the Zirid king Abd Allah, Badis's grandson, traces the rising in his memoirs, the Tibyan, to Joseph's dealings with Ibn Sumadih of Almeria and never mentions the poem, and Emilio García Gómez, who first edited the poet's diwan, wrote that the poem set Granada alight but judged it only the spark for something already in the air, and thought the massacre would have happened without it.

translation: Tell the Sanhaja, every one of them,
full moons of the assembly, lions of the den:
1.sharh: The poet calls on the whole Sanhaja, the tribe whose chiefs ruled Granada, and flatters them before making his case: moons of their gatherings in rank, lions in their lairs in courage.

translation: Your lord has made a slip,
one that gladdens the eyes of those who gloat.
2.sharh: Their lord, Badis, has made a mistake that delights everyone who wishes the Sanhaja ill. The poet holds back what the mistake is until the next line.

translation: He chose an unbeliever for his secretary
when, had he wished, he could have had a Muslim.
3.sharh: The mistake: Badis gave the office to a non-Muslim when he could have chosen a Muslim. In al-Andalus at the time the king's secretary was his chief minister, as al-Maqqari notes.

translation: Through him the Jews grew mighty and swaggered;
they turned arrogant, who had been among the lowliest.
4.sharh: With one of their own running the state, the poet says, the Jews of Granada gained power and pride, though he counts them among the lowliest of people.

translation: They got what they wished and passed every bound;
so the hour of ruin has come, and they do not perceive it.
5.sharh: Having got all they wanted and gone past every limit, they are close to destruction without knowing it: an open threat. “And they do not perceive” echoes the Quran on punishment that comes unawares.

translation: How many a Muslim, virtuous and devout,
answers to the vilest ape among the idolaters.
6.sharh: Devout Muslims, he complains, now answer to Jewish officials, whom he insults as apes and calls idolaters. The verb is left unsaid; the sense is “serves” or “bows to”.

translation: None of this came of their own efforts:
the one who helps them rises from among us.
7.sharh: The Jews did not reach this position on their own; the help came from a Muslim, Badis himself. The blame falls first on the king who raised them.

translation: Why did he not follow, in dealing with them,
the good and God-fearing leaders who came before,
8.sharh: The poet reproaches Badis for not treating the Jews as earlier Muslim rulers had. The next lines describe that treatment as he sees it.

translation: and put them in the place they deserve,
and thrust them back to the lowest of the low?
9.sharh: Badis should have kept them in the low rank the poet thinks they deserve. The second half borrows the Quran's “then We reduced him to the lowest of the low” (95:5).

translation: They went about among us with their dues,
abased, humbled and despised,
10.sharh: This, the poet says, is how Jews lived under earlier rulers: going about among Muslims paying their dues, humbled. Al-Daya hears in it the Quran's verse on the poll tax paid “in humility” (9:29).

translation: and swept the rubbish heaps for a rag,
a dyed one, to wrap their buried dead.
11.sharh: They scoured the rubbish heaps, he says, for a coloured rag to shroud their dead: his picture of their poverty and abasement in those days. Shawqi Dayf's paraphrase has “soiled” for “dyed”.

translation: They did not belittle our leading men
or lord it over the righteous,
12.sharh: In those days, the poet says, Jews did not dare slight Muslim scholars and notables or lord it over pious men. He is accusing Joseph's circle of doing both.

translation: nor sit with them, a blemish on any gathering,
nor ride with them among the inner circle.
13.sharh: Nor, he says, did they sit with notables, where he thinks them a disgrace, or ride with the ruler's intimates in his train, as Joseph and his people now did.

translation: Badis, you are a shrewd man:
your guesses hit upon certainty itself.
14.sharh: Turning to Badis himself, the poet praises his sharpness: his guesses land on the truth. The praise prepares the reproach that follows.

translation: How then has what they are escaped you,
when horns are blown about them across the land?
15.sharh: A king so shrewd ought to see what they are, he argues, when their doings are proclaimed throughout the country as if by trumpets; what everyone knows cannot be hidden from him.

translation: And how can you love the spawn of fornication
when they have made you hated by all the world?
16.sharh: He insults the Jews as bastards and asks how Badis can love people who, he claims, have made the king hateful to everyone by what they do in his name.

translation: How can your ascent be completed
if you build and they tear down?
17.sharh: No ruler can rise if his ministers undo his work. The king builds his state while, the poet claims, Joseph's people pull it down behind him. The line recalls a famous verse attributed to Salih ibn Abd al-Quddus: “When will a building ever be finished, if you build it and another tears it down?”

translation: And how could you rest your trust in a sinner
and keep him at your side, a wretched companion?
18.sharh: He asks how Badis could trust the vizier, whom he calls a reprobate, and keep him close. “A wretched companion” is the Quran's phrase (43:38) for the comrade who leads a man astray.

translation: God has sent down in His revelation
a warning against the company of sinners.
19.sharh: He appeals to scripture: the Quran warns believers against befriending the wicked. Al-Daya points to 9:96, “God is not pleased with the wicked”.

translation: So take none of them into your service;
leave them to the curse of those who curse.
20.sharh: Badis should employ no Jew in his administration, the kind of service al-Daya says is meant, and leave them to be cursed. “Those who curse” echoes the Quran (2:159).

translation: The earth itself cries out at their sinfulness
and has all but heaved beneath every one of us.
21.sharh: In his hyperbole the earth groans under the sins he lays at their door and nearly shakes everyone off it. The verb, tamid, is the Quran's for the earth that the mountains keep from heaving (16:15).

translation: Look with your own eyes across its regions:
you will find them there, dogs driven off in disgrace.
22.sharh: He urges Badis to see for himself, and insults the Jews as dogs. Khasi'in, “driven off, abject”, is the Quran's word for the Sabbath-breakers turned into apes (2:65).

translation: How is it that you alone have drawn them close
when everywhere else they are kept at a distance,
23.sharh: He presents Badis as the only ruler to bring Jews into his inner circle when, he says, everywhere else they are kept far from power. Ihsan Abbas, though, quotes a poet of Denia complaining of a Jewish tax collector there.

translation: though you are the king all approve,
scion of kings, of a glorious line,
24.sharh: The poet softens the reproach with praise: Badis is a king his people accept, born of noble kings, which makes his choice all the harder to understand.

translation: and you lead the field among mankind,
as you rank among the foremost of the great?
25.sharh: More praise: Badis outstrips other men and stands among the foremost. Ihsan Abbas notes that the poet praises the king to win his trust.

translation: When I came to live in Granada,
I saw them there, running riot.
26.sharh: Now the poet speaks as an eyewitness: living in Granada, he says, he saw the Jews doing as they pleased with its affairs.

translation: They have shared out the city and its districts:
in every place there is one of them, accursed.
27.sharh: He claims the Jews have divided Granada and its provinces among themselves, “an accursed one” in every post. Ibn Idhari records that Joseph appointed Jews to administrative offices.

translation: They collect its taxes;
they chomp and they nibble.
28.sharh: They gather the taxes, he complains, and then devour them, greedily and to the last scrap: they take everything. Ihsan Abbas notes that the taxes went to the treasury, not to the collectors, though no one then stopped to consider it.

translation: They wear the finest clothes,
and you go dressed in the meanest.
29.sharh: He sets their fine clothes against the poor dress of the Muslims, now speaking directly to the Sanhaja and the people of Granada.

translation: They are the keepers of your secrets,
but how can a traitor be trusted?
30.sharh: The Jews now hold the state's secrets; the poet asks how a traitor can be a trusted keeper, and so accuses them of treachery.

translation: Let anyone else devour a single dirham
and he is sent away; they, when they devour, are drawn closer.
31.sharh: “Eating” money is embezzling it. An official who takes one coin is dismissed, the poet complains, while Jewish officials who do the same are favoured.

translation: They have risen against you over your Lord,
and you neither stop them nor object.
32.sharh: He accuses them of attacking the Muslims' faith itself, and the Muslims of doing nothing to prevent it or even to protest.

translation: They have beguiled you with their sorceries,
so that you neither hear nor see.
33.sharh: He claims Joseph's people have bewitched the Sanhaja, the people of Granada and the king, or deceived them so cleverly that it works like magic, as al-Daya glosses it.

translation: They do the slaughtering in its markets,
and you eat the extremities.
34.sharh: The Jews control the butchering in Granada's markets, he says, and leave the Muslims the extremities, the head and feet, the poorest parts of the animal.

translation: Their ape has faced his house with marble
and brought the clear water of springs to it,
35.sharh: Now he turns to the vizier himself, “their ape”, and his luxury: a house faced with marble and fed by spring water. Ihsan Abbas reads these lines as an attack on Joseph's opulence.

translation: so that our needs now lie with him,
and we stand waiting at his door.
36.sharh: Muslims who want anything done must now wait at the vizier's door, a reversal the poet finds humiliating after his picture of the Jews' place under earlier rulers (lines 10–13).

translation: He laughs at us and at our religion:
to our Lord we shall return.
37.sharh: The vizier, he claims, mocks the Muslims and their faith, and the poet answers with the words Muslims say at a calamity. Ihsan Abbas suggests an allusion to a treatise by Ibn Naghrela criticising the Quran, which he thinks Joseph rather than his father wrote, and which Ibn Hazm refuted.

translation: If you said of his wealth
that it is like your own, you would be telling the truth.
38.sharh: Joseph's fortune, the poet argues, came from the state's revenues, so Badis may treat it as his own. Al-Daya explains it as leave to take the money back into the treasury.

translation: Hurry to slaughter him as an offering to God;
sacrifice him, for he is a fat ram.
39.sharh: Here the poem demands the vizier's death outright, presenting the killing as a pious sacrifice, like a fat ram offered at the feast. Joseph was killed in the rising of Safar 459 AH (December 1066 CE).

translation: Do not lift the pressure from his people:
they have hoarded every precious thing.
40.sharh: The incitement widens from the vizier to his community: keep them under pressure, the poet urges, since he claims they have hoarded every treasure.

translation: Break up their hostile band and take their wealth:
you have more right to what they amass.
41.sharh: He urges Badis to break up the Jewish community and seize its property, which he says belongs by right to the king. After Joseph's killing, Ibn Idhari and Abd Allah record, the rioters plundered the houses and wealth of Granada's Jews.

translation: Do not think killing them a breach of faith:
the breach would be to leave them to their mischief.
42.sharh: The poet meets in advance the objection that killing protected non-Muslims would break faith with them, and turns it around. Ihsan Abbas notes the weight this ruling carried, coming from a jurist known for his piety.

translation: They have broken the covenant we made with them,
so how can you be blamed for dealing with those who break it?
43.sharh: His argument is legal: by gaining power over Muslims, he holds, the Jews broke the terms of the pact that protected them, and so lost its protection.

translation: And how can they keep their protection
while we sink unknown and they stand on top?
44.sharh: For the poet, protected status assumed that non-Muslims stood below Muslims. With the Muslims sunk in obscurity and the Jews prominent, he argues, the pact no longer holds.

translation: We are the ones abased among them,
as if we were the wrongdoers and they the righteous.
45.sharh: The Muslims, he complains, are humiliated among the Jews as though they had done wrong and the Jews right. Al-Daya takes it as aimed at the vizier's harshness and the men he employed.

translation: So do not accept what they do to us,
for you are held to account for their deeds.
46.sharh: He warns Badis that he appointed these men and so will answer to God for what they do to the Muslims.

translation: Mind your God in how you treat His party,
for the party of God are the victors.
47.sharh: The poem ends by telling Badis to fear God in his treatment of the Muslims, God's own party, and quotes the Quran's promise that “the party of God are the victors” (5:56).

1.1.3.head: صِنهاجَة
1.1.3.meaning: Sanhaja: a great Berber tribal confederation. The Zirid kings of Granada, Badis among them, were Sanhaja.

1.2.2.head: النَّدِيّ
1.2.2.meaning: Nadiyy: the gathering where a tribe sits and talks.

3.1.2.head: كاتِب
3.1.2.meaning: Katib: secretary; in al-Andalus, the king's chief minister. Here Joseph ibn Naghrela, who succeeded his father Samuel as Badis's vizier.

6.2.2.head: قِرد
6.2.2.meaning: Ape: an insult that draws on the Quran's story of the Sabbath-breakers told “Be apes, despised” (2:65).

6.2.4.head: المُشرِك
6.2.4.meaning: Mushrik: one who gives God partners, an idolater; the poet applies it to the Jews.

10.1.3.head: أَخراج
10.1.3.meaning: Akhraj: dues, tribute, as al-Daya explains it; or saddlebags, the packs of pedlars, as Shawqi Dayf reads it.

11.2.2-3.meaning: “The covering of the buried”: a shroud.

13.1.4.head: هُجنَة
13.1.4.meaning: Hujna: a blemish, a thing to be ashamed of.

14.1.1.head: باديس
14.1.1.meaning: Badis: Badis ibn Habbus, Zirid king of Granada, who died in 465 AH (1073 CE).

15.2.5.meaning: Horns: here the horns blown as trumpets to proclaim something.

26.1.3.head: غَرناطَة
26.1.3.meaning: Granada: the capital of the Zirid kings, which grew as nearby Elvira fell into ruin.

27.1.3.head: أَعمال
27.1.3.meaning: A'mal: the districts and towns governed from a city.

28.2.2.head: خَضَمَ
28.2.2.meaning: Khadm: eating with the back teeth, with the whole mouth.

28.2.4.head: قَضَمَ
28.2.4.meaning: Qadm: eating with the front teeth, nibbling.

29.2.2.head: أَوضَع
29.2.2.meaning: Awda': meanest, lowliest. Inan and Ihsan Abbas print awda'iha, “its humblest kinds”.

35.2.3-4.meaning: “The sweet water of springs”: clear, fresh spring water.

37.2.1-4.meaning: From the Quran (2:156), “We belong to God and to Him we return”, said at news of a death or calamity.

39.1.4.head: قُربَة
39.1.4.meaning: Qurba: an act that brings one closer to God.

41.1.2.head: عِدى
41.1.2.meaning: Ida: enemies, read by al-Daya as their hostile band. His earlier edition and Inan have urahum, “their bonds”.

43.1.3.head: عَهد
43.1.3.meaning: The covenant: the dhimma, the pact under which Jews and Christians in Muslim lands kept their lives, property and religion in return for the poll tax.

44.1.4.head: ذِمَّة
44.1.4.meaning: Dhimma: protection, the covenant of protection.

46.2.2.head: رَهين
46.2.2.meaning: Rahin: held in pledge, answerable; as in the Quran, “every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned” (74:38).

47.1.4.head: حِزب
47.1.4.meaning: Hizb: party, faction; the party of God are the believers.
